(b)  The specific enforcement of monetary obligations
The specific enforcement of monetary obligations is enshrined in new article 1341, 
which confirms that the right of the injured party to performance under new article 
1221 extends to debt claims,29 leaving unaltered the position prior to the reforms.30
It is an unfettered right, in that the contract price can be claimed in preference to
other remedies such as compensatory damages and termination.31 There does not
appear to be any discretion in the court as to the appropriateness of the remedy. As 
the Cour de cassation held in one case, ‘a creditor always has the right to prefer the
payment of the price to an award of damages or termination of the contract’.32
An example is a case in which a student entered into a contract with a teaching 
institution to receive long-​distance classes over a six-​year period. He had to pay an 
enrolment fee of thirty francs and thirty-​five monthly course fees of forty francs. 
Nine months after starting the course, he sought to terminate the contract. The 
Cour de cassation quashed the refusal of the lower court to order payment of the 
monthly fees for the remaining twenty-​six months of the term, holding that the in­
stitution was entitled to recover the entire balance of the fees.
One means by which the injured party can be impeded in recovering the con­
tract price is the délai de grâce.33 Where the defaulting party is in financial dif­
ficulty, new article 1343-​5 of the Civil Code confers a discretion on the court to 
extend time for payment of the sum due by up to two years. It states in its first three 
paragraphs as follows:
29	 See also paragraph 1 of article L111-​1 of the Code of Civil Enforcement Procedures.
30	 Laithier, ‘Exécution Forcée en Nature’ (n 28) 269.
31	 Deshayes, Genicon, and Laithier (n 10) 638 have questioned whether the proportionality require­
ment in article 1221 of the Civil Code applies to the specific enforcement of monetary obligations. If it 
were to do so, the injured party may not be entitled to the agreed price where termination and compen­
satory damages would be adequate remedies and significantly less costly to the defaulting party. The 
requirement is not referred to in article 1341, suggesting that it does not apply. For P Malaurie, L Aynès, 
and P Stoffel-​Munck, Droit des obligations (10th edn, LGDJ: Paris, 2018) [1136], even after the reforms, 
the injured party can prefer payment of the price over damages or termination. Some authors do not 
refer to any limitation on the right to obtain payment: F Terré, P Simler, Y Lequette, and F Chénedé, 
Droit civil: les obligations (12th edn, Dalloz: Paris, 2018), and Chantepie and Latina (n 13). See also 
Laithier, ‘Exécution Forcée en Nature’ (n 28) 269. It therefore appears that the limitation is understood 
by French lawyers not to apply in this context.
	
32	 Civ (1) 9 July 2003, JCP 2004.I.163, no 4, obs G Viney; RTD civ 2003.709, obs J Mestre and B Fages; 
M Fabre-​Magnan, Droit des Obligations, Contrat et engagement unilateral (2nd edn, PUF: Paris, 2010) 
[215]. See, however, Com 22 Oct 1996, Bull civ IV no 260. This decision has been rationalized on the 
ground that the lower court had accepted, albeit wrongly, that the contract could be terminated unilat­
erally by the promisor: RTD civ 1997.123, obs J Mestre and P Jourdain 439; D 1997 Somm 173, obs R 
Libchaber.
	
33	 A Sériaux, ‘Réflexions sur les délais de grâce’, RTD civ 1993.789; Laithier, ‘Exécution Forcée 
en Nature’ (n 28) 267–​8. For a detailed account in English on the délai de grace, see S Whittaker, ‘A 
Period of Grace for Contractual Performance?’ in M Andenas et al. (eds), Liber Amicorum Guido 
Alpa, Private Law Beyond the National Systems (British Institute of International and Comparative 
Law: London, 2007).
